name: Mary of Egypt

seo.title: Mary of Egypt: the door that would not open, and 47 years alone
seo.description: Mary of Egypt in plain words: her own story of lust and repentance, the church door, the lion at her grave, her feast days, and what scholars make of it.

band.where: Alexandria, Jerusalem and the desert beyond the Jordan
band.lede: The runaway of Alexandria who was stopped at a church door, and spent 47 years alone in the desert.

who: Mary of Egypt is known from one famous *Life*, read aloud in Orthodox churches every Lent. She ran away to Alexandria at twelve and lived seventeen years in lust. In Jerusalem an unseen force kept her out of a church. She repented, crossed the Jordan and lived 47 years alone in the desert.

tidbits.text: About a third of her *Life* is her own story, told to Zosimas in her own voice. Maria Kouli, who translated the Greek in 1996, puts it at “perhaps one-third of the whole”.

cite.text: Maria Kouli, introduction to the Life, in Holy Women of Byzantium (Dumbarton Oaks, 1996)

tidbits.text: In 872 an ancient Roman temple beside the Tiber was made into a church of St Mary of Egypt. It still stands by the Piazza della Bocca della Verità.

cite.text: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

tidbits.text: The Coptic book of saints gives her whole span: born about 345, died in 421. “All the years of her life were seventy six years.”

cite.text: Coptic synaxarium, 6 Baramouda

tidbits.text: Russians call the Thursday service where her *Life* is read the Standing of St Mary of Egypt. The canon sung with it is long, and heard standing.

cite.text: OrthoChristian, The Standing of St. Mary of Egypt

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In **Egypt**, probably about 344, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. The *Life* names no town. The Coptic book of saints makes her a child of Christian parents in Alexandria.

facts.label: Lived
facts.text: In **Alexandria** from the age of twelve, for seventeen years. Then briefly in **Jerusalem**, and 47 years in the desert east of the **Jordan**.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: Alone in the desert, on the night of her last communion: **1 April**, in the Greek *Life*. The year is unknown. The Bollandists said 421. Many others put it a century later.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: Where she died, by the monk **Zosimas**. A lion dug the grave, the *Life* says.

facts.label: Her Life
facts.text: Told by Zosimas to his monks and written down by another hand. The manuscripts name **Sophronius**, patriarch of Jerusalem, who died in 638. Some scholars doubt it.

facts.label: Relics
facts.text: Honoured at **Rome**, **Naples**, **Cremona**, **Antwerp** and other places, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Mary the Egyptian**, and in Latin {la|Maria Aegyptiaca}. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* calls her Mary of Egypt, “surnamed the Sinner”.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Nothing. She told Zosimas she had never learned to read.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In icons, a thin, sun-darkened woman in the cloak Zosimas gave her, often taking communion from him. In the West, often with her **loaves**, as Ribera painted her above.

facts.label: Her Sunday
facts.text: The fifth Sunday of **Great Lent**, in the Orthodox Church, the last before Palm Sunday. In 2027 it falls on **18 April**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to the Orthodox, Catholics and Copts. The Episcopal Church remembers her too.

portrait.alt: A dark oil painting: a young woman in a white dress and a blue mantle kneels on church steps among a crowd, looking up with one arm stretched out toward the Mother of God, who appears in the clouds with the Christ Child in a golden halo

portrait.creator: Luca Giordano
portrait.caption: Luca Giordano painted her turning point: kept out of the church, she looks up to the Mother of God. In the *Life* it is an icon; here it is a vision. Museum of Fine Arts, Ghent. Public domain.

gallery.alt: A Russian icon on a gold-brown board: two gaunt saints in long golden cloaks stand barefoot on a rocky slope, a bearded man at left and Mary of Egypt at right with her hands raised in prayer, with a pink city behind them and the Mother of God with the Christ Child in a round medallion of clouds above

gallery.creator: Yakov Kazanets
gallery.caption: Yakov Kazanets, 1648: Mary of Egypt (right) with Alexius the Man of God, under the Mother of God. The icon was painted for the wedding of Tsar Alexei and Maria Miloslavskaya, whose name saints they were. Public domain.

west.text: The **1916 Roman Martyrology**, and the older Catholic books.
The **Episcopal Church**, in *Lesser Feasts and Fasts*. The old Roman calendar also kept her on this day.

east.text: The **OCA** and the other Orthodox churches on the new calendar.
The **Russian Church** and others on the old calendar. Also the **Coptic** Church, on 6 Baramouda in its own calendar.

feasts.note: Why so many days? The Greek *Life* says she died on 1 April. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* thought the Western 2 and 3 April might be the days her relics reached the West. Churches on the old calendar keep 1 April thirteen days later, on 14 April, which is also the Coptic day. The Orthodox give her a Sunday too, the fifth of Great Lent. It moves with Easter: in 2027 it falls on **18 April**.

traits.title: frank about her past
traits.text: She did not dress her story up, and she expected Zosimas to run from it: “thou wilt soon flee from me in the manner in which a man may flee from an adder”. She told it anyway: “I will relate all to thee, concealing nothing”. She asked only that he keep praying for her.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

traits.title: all or nothing
traits.text: She did nothing by halves, in sin or out of it. When she heard of the pilgrim ship, she threw down her spindle and ran to the sea. When she heard the voice at the church, she set off for the Jordan the same day: “I ran continually, still weeping, upon my journey”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

traits.title: stubborn in the fight
traits.text: For seventeen years in the desert she longed for her old life. Each time, she threw herself on the ground and would not get up until the struggle passed. “I then beheld light shining all around me; and soon after a steadfast peace came to me.”

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

traits.title: humble before a priest
traits.text: She had walked on water, and Zosimas tried to kneel to her. She called from the river to stop him:“Know that thou art God's priest, and hast with thee the divine mysteries.” At their first meeting too, she insisted that he bless her, not she him.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

traits.title: taught without books
traits.text: She quoted the Scriptures so freely that Zosimas asked where she had learned the Psalms. She smiled. “Nor did I ever learn to read, nor ever listened to any of those people who pondered and read. But the word of God is quick and sharp, teaching this human intelligence within me.”

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

traits.title: content with almost nothing
traits.text: Zosimas brought her a basket of figs, dates and soaked lentils. She took three lentils with the tip of her finger, and said that “such a gift sufficed for one who kept her soul steadfast in purity”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

said.lede: No one wrote about her in her lifetime. These are the voices that kept her story, from the monk who found her to the scholars of today.

quotes.q: Blessed be God, Who alone worketh manifold wonders; and blessed be Thou, O Lord God, Who hast shewn me the gloriousness that Thou givest to them that dread Thee.
quotes.who: The monk Zosimas, when she had finished her story

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

quotes.q: We read in the life of St Mary of Egypt that she prayed before the statue of Our Lady and besought her intercession, and so obtained leave to enter the Church.
quotes.who: John of Damascus, defending icons, in the 700s. Mary Allies, his translator in 1898, wrote “statue”; the Greek *Life* speaks of an icon.

cite.text: John of Damascus, On Holy Images, tr. Mary H. Allies (1898)

quotes.q: By the arm, which, from the portal, warning, thrust me back again; by the forty years' repentance in the lonely desert-land; by the blissful farewell sentence which I wrote upon the sand!
quotes.who: Goethe gave her a speech in the last scene of *Faust* (1832), where she and two other penitent women plead before the Mother of God. Bayard Taylor's translation, 1871.

cite.text: Goethe, Faust, Part Two, Act 5, tr. Bayard Taylor

quotes.q: …if such a licentious woman could find forgiveness, surely ordinary sinners could hope for salvation.
quotes.who: Maria Kouli, on why her story was loved, 1996

cite.text: Maria Kouli, introduction to the Life, in Holy Women of Byzantium (Dumbarton Oaks, 1996)

quotes.q: …an example of repentance categorized by continual self-emptying, as opposed to a realized state of sanctity.
quotes.who: The Episcopal Church's calendar, on why the Orthodox read her *Life* in Lent

cite.text: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 3 April

moments.title: A runaway
moments.text: She had a home and a brother in Egypt. At twelve she left them for Alexandria, the great port. In her own words: “in the twelfth year of my age, I began to despise their love and betook myself to the city of Alexandria”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.title: Not for money
moments.text: She is plain about what followed, and firm on one point. She took no payment: “Neither did I lose my virginity for any man's presents, nor would I indeed receive anything from any one who desired to give me somewhat”. She lived poor and spun flax. What drove her was desire, and she called it living: “this I accounted as life”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.title: The pilgrim ship
moments.text: One day she saw crowds running to the sea. They were sailing to Jerusalem for the feast of the Holy Cross. She had no fare. She would pay with her body, she told a young man, and he walked off laughing. So she went down to the shore and talked her way onto a ship full of young men. Of the voyage she said little: “I wonder how the sea could suffer and endure my unrighteous desires”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.when: The feast of the Cross, 14 September
moments.title: The door
moments.text: On the feast the crowds pushed into the church to see the wood of the Cross. She pushed in with them. At the threshold something held her back, while everyone else went in. She tried three or four times, until she was worn out: “Just as if some strong company of men opposed me to prevent my entrance, so the sudden vengeance of God barred the door to me”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints; Kouli (1996), on the date of the feast

moments.title: The icon
moments.text: Alone in a corner of the porch, she understood why. She wept and beat her breast. Above her she saw an icon of the Mother of God, and asked her help: let her in to see the Cross, and she would give up her old life. John of Damascus quoted her vow from the Greek *Life*: “When I see the Cross of thy Son, I will at once renounce the world and the things of the world, and forthwith follow wherever thou shalt lead.” This time she walked in freely.

cite.text: John of Damascus, On Holy Images, tr. Mary H. Allies (1898); the Life, in Skeat's edition

moments.title: Three coins, three loaves
moments.text: Back at the icon, she heard a voice: “If thou wilt pass over the river Jordan, there thou shalt experience and find good rest.” A stranger gave her three coins, and she bought three loaves. By sunset she reached the church of St John the Baptist by the river. She washed her hands and face in the Jordan, received communion, ate half a loaf and slept. Early next morning she crossed over.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.title: The long fight
moments.text: Her clothes rotted away, and she lived on her loaves, then on roots. The hardest part was inside her. For seventeen years she longed for the wine, the meat and the songs of Alexandria. Like Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 11:5), she remembered the food of Egypt: “I yearned for the fishes that were in Egypt”. Then, she said, “the holy Mother of God aided me and directed my ways”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.title: Found by Zosimas
moments.text: Each Lent the monks of a monastery near the Jordan went out into the desert, each man alone. One year the old priest Zosimas saw a figure far off: “she was very swart of body by reason of the sun's heat, and the locks of her head were as white as wool”. It fled, and he ran after it, calling. She stopped across a dry stream bed and called him by name, though they had never met. She asked for his cloak, having no clothes. Then she told him everything.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.title: Her last communion
moments.text: She made him promise two things: to tell no one of her while she lived, and to bring her communion at the Jordan on Holy Thursday the next year. He came with the sacrament in a little cup. She crossed the river to him, said the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, received communion, and prayed Simeon's prayer. Then she asked him to come back in a year to the place where they had first met.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

moments.title: Written down
moments.text: When he had buried her, Zosimas went home and told the monks everything. They kept the day of her death: they “magnified the day of her happy departure with awe and love and much faith”. The story passed from monk to monk until it was written down. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says it was written “by one who states that he learned the details from the monks of the monastery to which Zosimus had belonged”.

cite.text: The Life, in Skeat's edition; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910)

miracles.lede: The *Life* tells its wonders plainly, as things Zosimas saw and she told. They are given here as the Old English *Life* tells them, in the English of Skeat's edition, with the doubts at the end. Its writer opens with a promise:

pledge.q: …may it never be that I should falsify the holy narratives or keep silence from speech.

cite.text: The Life, prologue, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

items.title: Raised as she prayed
items.text: She turned east, lifted her arms and prayed without a sound. Zosimas looked up from the ground and saw her standing on the air.
items.quote: he saw her lifted up, as it were the space of a man's ell, above the earth, and began to pray hanging in the air
items.witness: Zosimas, who swore to it with God as his witness. The *Golden Legend* makes it “well nigh a foot and a half”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

items.title: Across the water
items.text: He waited on the bank, wondering how she would cross with no boat. By moonlight he saw her make the sign of the cross over the river and step onto it.
items.quote: So she went towards him, walking on the soft waves as if on dry land.
items.witness: Zosimas alone. She went back over the water the same way.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

items.title: Letters in the earth
items.text: He found her dead, and did not know even her name. Then he saw writing on the ground by her head. It gave her name, and asked him to bury her. But she had told him she had never learned to read.
items.quote: When the old man had read the letters, he first of all looked to see who had written them

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

items.title: The lion
items.text: He had no spade, and the ground was too hard for the stick he found. Looking up, he saw a huge lion by her body. He made the sign of the cross. The lion came to him gently, and at his word dug the grave with its claws.
items.quote: Then began the lion to fawn upon the old man, and greeted him with its moving limbs.
items.witness: Zosimas. When the grave was filled, the lion went off into the desert “like the gentlest lamb”.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

more.title: The door that held her back
more.text: Her own account of the church door in Jerusalem. The others went in freely:
more.quote: the divine might prevented me from going in, and I was soon thrust out from amid all the people

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

more.title: She knew him
more.text: She called Zosimas by name and knew he was a priest, though no one had told her. She also knew the rule of his monastery, and sent its abbot word of what to set right there.
more.quote: he manifestly perceived that she was enlightened with divine foreknowledge

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

more.title: Kept at home, as she said
more.text: She told him that next Lent he would not be able to leave his monastery, even if he wanted to. When Lent came he fell ill, and stayed behind.
more.quote: he himself was left in the minster, and there remained kept in by a bodily infirmity

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

more.title: Twenty days in an hour
more.text: The writing by her body showed she had died the very night of her communion at the Jordan. So she had crossed, in an hour, the desert it took Zosimas weeks to walk.
more.quote: the journey which Zosimus had performed with much toil in twenty days, all that Mary had fulfilled in the course of an hour

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

doubt.title: The lion's older twin
doubt.text: The lion has a famous forerunner. In Jerome's *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, written in the 300s, Antony finds the old hermit Paul dead. He too has nothing to dig with: “Antony began to lament that he had no implement for digging the ground”. Then “two lions from the recesses of the desert” come and dig the grave. The scholar Maria Kouli sees the likeness as no accident. The lion, she writes, is one of many passages suggesting that “the composition was strongly influenced by Jerome's vita of Paul the Hermit”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1910 kept its distance too: Zosimas buried her “aided, we are told, by a lion”.

cites.text: Jerome, Life of Paulus the First Hermit, tr. W. H. Fremantle (1893)
Maria Kouli, introduction to the Life, in Holy Women of Byzantium (1996); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910)

extras.title: Story or history?
extras.lede: The Church has read her *Life* as a true story for thirteen centuries. Scholars are less sure. Here is each side, in its own words.

items.title: No dates to hold
items.text: The *Life* gives her age at each stage, and almost nothing else to date it by. So her dates float. The Bollandists, the Jesuit scholars of the saints, put her death in 421. Others put it a century later. Maria Kouli, who translated the Greek *Life* in 1996, goes further:
items.quote: it is impossible to provide a chronology for the life of Mary, or even to establish her historicity

cite.text: Kouli, Holy Women of Byzantium (1996); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910)

items.title: An older, simpler story
items.text: In the 500s Cyril of Scythopolis told of a monk named John who found a woman living alone in a cave in the Judean desert. She said she had been a singer at the church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem, and had fled so as not to lead men astray. She lived eighteen years on a jar of water and a basket of beans. When John came back, she was dead, and he buried her. John Moschos told a similar tale. Kouli thinks the longer *Life* grew from such stories. There were real women hermits in those deserts, she adds, and:
items.quote: one of them may well have inspired the edifying tale of Mary of Egypt

cite.text: Kouli, Holy Women of Byzantium (1996), after Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of Kyriakos

items.title: Who wrote it
items.text: The manuscripts name Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem from 634 to 638. The medieval writer Zonaras and the scholar Hippolyte Delehaye accepted that. Others, among them François Halkin, doubted it. Kouli thinks it was probably written in the 600s either way, since John of Damascus quoted it in the 700s. The Bollandists thought it older still. In the words of the *Catholic Encyclopedia*:
items.quote: the Bollandists give good reasons for believing that the Life was written before 500

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Kouli, Holy Women of Byzantium (1996)

items.title: What the churches say
items.text: The churches keep her for what the story teaches: that no one is past repentance. The Orthodox read the *Life* aloud in church in the fifth week of Lent. The Episcopal Church's calendar is frank about the source: most of what is known of her, it says, comes from the *Life*. Its prayer for her day asks that, like her, we may not leave this life until we understand
items.quote: the ways of repentance and the benefits of prayer

cite.text: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 3 April

words.note: She wrote nothing, and said she could not read. Her words come through the *Life*, which says Zosimas told them to his monks. They are given here in the English of Skeat's edition of the Old English *Life*, and once as John of Damascus quoted the Greek.

feature.kicker: Asked how she lived with no food or clothes
feature.q: Verily I am fed to the full with sufficient sustenance, that is to say, with the promise of my salvation; and I am clothed upon with the protecting garment of the word of God
feature.ctx: Then she quoted Jesus: man does not live by bread alone, but by every word from the mouth of God.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

quotes.q: I am a sinful woman, though endued, nevertheless, with holy baptism; and I am no spirit, but embers and ashes, and all flesh.
quotes.who: When Zosimas feared she was a ghost

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

quotes.q: Of a truth I blush — pardon me, father abbot — to tell thee the vileness of my deeds
quotes.who: Before she told him her story

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

quotes.q: Believe me, I have never seen anyone but thee or wild beasts, nor creature of any kind since I passed over the water of Jordan and arrived hither in this wilderness
quotes.who: Asked if she had learned the Psalms

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

quotes.q: Tell also John, the abbot of the minster in which thou art, diligently to take heed to himself and to his flock also, because that there are some customs there for him to set right and to improve.

cite.text: The Life, tr. in Skeat's edition of Ælfric's Lives of Saints

quotes.q: O loving Queen, thou hast shown me thy goodness; thou didst not despise the petition of my unworthiness.
quotes.who: To the Mother of God, when she came out of the church. From the Greek, as John of Damascus quoted it; tr. Mary H. Allies, 1898

cite.text: John of Damascus, On Holy Images, tr. Mary H. Allies (1898)

myths.truth: Many books say so. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* speaks of “a life of public prostitution”, and the Episcopal Church's calendar calls her “an Alexandrian prostitute”. In her own story she insists on the opposite: she refused money. “Nor do thou suppose that I would receive anything for any world's wealth, but ever lived in poverty”. She did once trade her body, for her fare to Jerusalem. The *Golden Legend* of the 1260s puts it more bluntly than the *Life*: she “refused no man”.

cite.text: The Life, in Skeat's edition; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; the Golden Legend

myths.claim: The penitent who lived for decades alone in the desert, lifted up at prayer, was Mary Magdalene.
myths.truth: That is Mary of Egypt's story. The Gospels give Mary Magdalene no desert. The medieval West gave her one. In the *Golden Legend* of the 1260s she lives thirty years alone in a wilderness in Provence, is lifted into the air at prayer, and takes a last communion from a bishop before she dies. Read side by side, the two stories are close: the *Legend* even has Magdalene raised from the ground “the space of two or three cubits”.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, the Life of S. Mary Magdalene, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis (1900)

circle.name: Zosimas
circle.text: A priest and monk of Palestine, in a monastery near the Jordan. He found her in the desert, gave her his cloak, brought her last communion and buried her. The Orthodox keep his day on 4 April.

cite.text: The Life; OCA, 1 April

circle.name: The Mother of God
circle.text: Mary prayed before her icon at the church door and chose her as her protector. In the desert, she said, the Mother of God helped her through her hardest years.

cite.text: The Life, in Skeat's edition; John of Damascus, On Holy Images

circle.name: John, the abbot
circle.text: Abbot of Zosimas's monastery. She sent him word that some customs there needed setting right, and he set them right.

cite.text: The Life, in Skeat's edition

circle.name: Sophronius of Jerusalem
circle.text: Patriarch of Jerusalem from 634 to 638. The manuscripts of her *Life* name him as its writer. Scholars are divided.

cite.text: Kouli, Holy Women of Byzantium (1996)

circle.name: Andrew of Crete
circle.text: Archbishop of Crete from the late 600s, who wrote the Great Canon, a long hymn of repentance. The Orthodox sing it whole on the Thursday of her week in Lent, when her *Life* is read.

cite.text: OCA, Saint Andrew of Crete; OrthoChristian

circle.name: Mary Magdalene
circle.text: A different Mary, of the Gospels. The medieval West gave Magdalene a desert life much like this one.

cite.text: The Golden Legend

death.big: She died alone in the desert, the night of her last communion. Zosimas found her a year later.
paras: He went back to the dry stream bed where they had first met. She lay dead, her hands folded, facing east. He washed her feet with his tears and did not dare touch anything else. He still did not know her name.

Then he saw writing on the ground by her head. It asked him to bury Mary, and said she had died the very night of her communion: on 1 April, in the Greek *Life*. A lion dug the grave. He buried her with only the torn piece of cloak he had once thrown her, and went home to tell the monks.

later.title: How her story travelled
later.text: The Greek *Life* was quoted by John of Damascus in the 700s and put into Latin by Paul, a deacon of Naples. From the Latin came the Old English *Life* quoted on this page, and the short version in the *Golden Legend*. Versions exist in Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic and Slavonic. The national library in Paris alone holds 37 Greek manuscripts of it.

saint.big: Yes. The Orthodox, Catholic and Coptic churches count her a saint, and the Episcopal Church remembers her.

churches.note: 1 April, and the fifth Sunday of Lent

paras: No pope or council ever declared her a saint. In the *Life*, her honour begins with the monks who first heard her story. It grew from there.

In the Orthodox Church she has a Sunday of her own, the fifth of Great Lent, the last before Palm Sunday. On the Thursday before it, the whole Great Canon of Andrew of Crete is sung, and her *Life* is read aloud in two parts. The Church's hymn for her day sums up why she is kept:
